screens.title: Translating ER Models to Relational Schemas and SQL DDL
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we move from abstract modeling to a working database schema. You'll learn how each entity and attribute in your ER diagram becomes a table and column, and how relationships turn into primary and foreign key constraints. Choosing the right S Q L data types is essential: they affect storage, precision, and query performance. We'll also cover constraints — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT — so the database enforces the rules you designed in the ERD. Concrete examples from customer-orders, employees, students-courses, and a library loan scenario show how to express one-to-many, one-to-one, and many-to-many relationships in DDL. Finally, you'll see how ALTER TABLE supports safe schema evolution and common pitfalls to avoid, such as missing foreign keys or incorrect data types. By the end of this lesson you will be able to write clear CREATE TABLE statements, pick suitable types, and implement keys and constraints so your schema is both correct and performant. Consider how the rules you add now will prevent application bugs later. Which integrity rule do you expect to be most important for your next schema?

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Translating ER Models
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Translate ERDs into robust relational schemas

This lesson shows how to express entities, attributes, and relationships as SQL DDL. Learn to select data types and add constraints that preserve integrity and performance for your applications.

Visual: Mapping Snapshot
Entity → Table
Attribute → Column
1:N → FK on many side
M:N → Junction table
Explore Key Topics
Data Types
Pick sizes and precision carefully to balance storage and accuracy.
Keys & Relationships
Express 1:1, 1:N, and M:N with PKs, FKs, and junction tables.
Constraints
NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT enforce business rules at the DB level.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to the practical steps you will take converting ER models into real tables. First, you will translate entities into tables and attributes into columns, choosing types that match expected values and scale. Second, you will convert ERD relationships into primary and foreign key constraints so referential integrity is enforced by the DBMS, handling common patterns like one-to-many, one-to-one, and many-to-many with junction tables. Third, you'll select S Q L data types appropriately — integers of the right size, precise decimals for money, and timestamp types for temporal data — to balance space and correctness. Fourth, you'll write CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE statements and apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT constraints to ensure the data meets business rules. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help remember when to use the pattern, and the verified competency milestone points to writing correct DDL for a simple library schema. Practicing these skills reduces runtime errors and prevents inconsistent data in applications. Which objective will you practice first?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied
screens.narratorSegment: These applied objectives show how you will use DDL in real scenarios. You will write CREATE TABLE statements for entities and specify NOT NULL for required fields like names or dates so applications can rely on consistent records. You will convert ERD relationships: place a foreign key on the many side for one-to-many patterns, use a unique foreign key for one-to-one, and create junction tables with composite primary keys for many-to-many. You will choose data types like BIGINT for global identifiers or DECIMAL for exact monetary values and apply CHECK constraints to guard against invalid values such as negative prices or out-of-range years. Finally, you will evolve schemas safely with ALTER TABLE, adding columns or constraints after testing in development. Each skill ties directly to the hands-on activity for a library system, where you'll write full CREATE TABLE statements and add checks and defaults. Practicing these tasks helps you catch integration bugs earlier and makes your schema self-documenting. Which applied objective will you try in the lab?

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Learning Objectives — Applied

Applied Objectives

Translate each objective into a concrete DDL task and verify it in a development database before production.

01 Create required fields

Use NOT NULL for fields that applications expect, such as title or borrowed_date. Prevents incomplete records.

Tool tip: test with sample INSERTs
02 Implement relationships

One-to-many uses FK on the many side; many-to-many needs a junction table with composite PK for uniqueness.

Tool tip: add FK constraints early
03 Choose types mindfully

Pick DECIMAL for money, TIMESTAMP for change tracking, and appropriate integer sizes for IDs.

Tool tip: check expected ranges
04 Evolve schema safely

Use ALTER TABLE in development to add columns or constraints, and plan for migrations and locks on large tables.

Tool tip: test offline on copies

screens.title: Entities to Tables — Mapping rules
screens.narratorSegment: Mapping entities to tables is the first concrete step when implementing an ER model. An entity becomes a table and each attribute becomes a column. Begin by choosing clear table names that reflect the modeled concept — for example Customers or Book — and use consistent column naming for keys like customer_id or ISBN. Decide which attributes are mandatory and add NOT NULL to those columns; fields such as title or borrowed_date are often required. Choose a primary key for each table: this can be a natural key like ISBN or a surrogate key like an auto-incrementing identifier. A practical example is the Book entity: map ISBN to a VARCHAR primary key of length 13, set title and author to VARCHAR with NOT NULL, and add a CHECK to ensure the publication year is valid. A common misconception is treating every attribute as nullable by default; required business fields should be NOT NULL to prevent incomplete records. Another pitfall is overusing TEXT or very large types where a bounded VARCHAR would be more efficient. Key takeaway: map entities systematically, apply NOT NULL for required attributes, and choose keys early so relationships can reference them. How will you name keys in your next schema?

keyIdea.title: Entity → Table
keyIdea.text: Convert each entity to a table, attributes to columns, pick a clear primary key, and apply NOT NULL where business rules require it.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Entities to Tables

Map entities and attributes into tables and columns

Define names, keys, and nullability to reflect the ERD’s intent and application requirements.

Rules
  • Entity → Table; Attribute → Column.
  • Pick a primary key; use natural keys when stable, otherwise use surrogate keys.
  • Apply NOT NULL for required business fields (e.g., title, name, borrowed_date).
  • Prefer bounded VARCHAR over TEXT for predictable lengths.
Example
Book entity: ISBN (VARCHAR(13) PK), title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, author VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, publication_year INT
Key Takeaway

Be deliberate with keys and nullability; this prevents incomplete data and simplifies FK references.

Scenario Walkthrough
Consider the library Book table. Choosing ISBN as VARCHAR(13) preserves the natural identifier and supports lookups by ISBN. If your system needs an internal numeric id for joins or performance, add a surrogate BIGINT as well, but keep ISBN as a unique key.
Common Mistake
Leaving essential fields nullable leads to logic errors in applications that assume those fields always exist.
Check Your Understanding
If a book title is mandatory, should title be NOT NULL? Why might you still keep an internal numeric id?

screens.title: Choosing SQL Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting data types is a balance between storage efficiency, precision, and correctness. Use integer types like INT or BIGINT for whole numbers; choose based on expected range — INT is fine for moderate ranges, BIGINT for very large global identifiers. For exact numeric values such as money, use DECIMAL or NUMERIC with a fixed precision and scale; floating-point types like FLOAT or REAL introduce rounding and are not recommended for financial data. Text attributes use VARCHAR with a reasonable upper bound, or TEXT where length is unpredictable. For temporal data pick DATE for dates only, TIME for time-only values, and TIMESTAMP or DATETIME for combined date-time; prefer timestamp types that include timezone when tracking global events. A concrete example: product price should be DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL; a username can be VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL. A common misconception is overusing the largest types by default; this wastes storage and can hide range problems until runtime. Another trap is using FLOAT for money, causing subtle calculation errors. Key takeaway: choose the smallest type that safely fits expected values and enforces necessary precision. What attributes in your schema need stricter precision controls?

keyIdea.text: Pick types that reflect value range and precision needs: integers for counts/IDs, DECIMAL for money, VARCHAR for bounded text, TIMESTAMP for datetimes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Choosing SQL Data Types

Choose types for range, precision, and semantics

Match each attribute’s nature — numeric, textual, temporal — to a type that enforces correctness and storage efficiency.

Numeric Types
INT / BIGINT / DECIMAL
  • INT, BIGINT: whole numbers; pick by expected range.
  • DECIMAL(p,s): exact values with scale, ideal for money.
  • FLOAT / REAL: approximate; avoid for financial data.
Text & Temporal
  • VARCHAR(n): bounded text for performance and validation.
  • TEXT: very long content when length unpredictable.
  • DATE/TIMESTAMP: use TIMESTAMP for event logging, DATE for birthdays.
Concrete Examples
CREATE TABLE Products (
  product_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  product_name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  stock_quantity INT CHECK (stock_quantity >= 0)
);
Common Mistake
Choosing FLOAT for currency can produce rounding errors in sums and comparisons.
Key Takeaway

Use DECIMAL for exact decimals, choose integer sizes by range, and bound text where possible for validation and performance.

screens.title: Primary Keys & Surrogate Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Primary keys uniquely identify rows and are central to relational integrity. A natural key is derived from domain data — for example ISBN uniquely identifies a book. A surrogate key is an artificial identifier, typically an auto-incrementing integer or serial. Surrogate keys simplify joins and can improve index performance, but they add an extra column and require a UNIQUE constraint on any natural identifier you still want to enforce. In many large systems, a BIGINT surrogate key is common because it avoids future overflow. Implementing auto-increment uses DBMS-specific features such as AUTO_INCREMENT, SERIAL, or IDENTITY. A concrete example: a Customers table might include customer_id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY while still marking email as UNIQUE NOT NULL. Misconceptions include thinking surrogate keys hide bad natural keys — surrogate keys are for identity, not for replacing unique business constraints. Another pitfall is using small integer types for IDs that will grow beyond their range. Key takeaway: choose a stable primary key strategy and enforce uniqueness on any business identifiers separately. How will you balance natural readability and long-term scalability in your keys?

keyIdea.title: Primary Key Strategy
keyIdea.text: Use natural keys when stable; prefer surrogate auto-increment keys for flexibility at scale, and enforce uniqueness on business identifiers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Primary Keys & Surrogates

Choose stable identifiers for rows

Decide whether to use a domain-derived key or a surrogate auto-incrementing key for primary identification.

Comparison: Natural vs Surrogate
Natural: readable, no extra column, but risky if domain values change.
Surrogate: stable, compact, good for joins; keep business uniqueness via UNIQUE constraints.
Process
  1. Decide if a domain value is stable and universal.
  2. If not, add a surrogate primary key (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT).
  3. Add UNIQUE on any business identifier you must preserve.
Example DDL
CREATE TABLE Customers (
  customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  first_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);
Pro Tip
Keep surrogate keys as the clustered or primary index, and create secondary unique indexes for business lookups like email.

screens.title: One-to-Many and Foreign Keys
screens.narratorSegment: One-to-many relationships are common: a single customer places many orders. To implement this, put the primary key of the one side into the many side as a foreign key. The foreign key column should be NOT NULL if every child row must relate to a parent, and you should add an explicit FOREIGN KEY constraint referencing the parent's primary key. This allows the DBMS to enforce referential integrity and prevents orphaned child rows. An example from the chapter: Orders includes customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL and a FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id). A practical misconception is assuming client code will prevent orphaned rows; without the FK, application bugs can create inconsistent data. Also consider cascade behaviors: ON DELETE CASCADE or ON DELETE SET NULL are decisions that affect data retention and must be chosen to match business rules. Key takeaway: model referential integrity in DDL using foreign keys, and explicitly decide cascading rules rather than relying on application logic. How will you handle deletions in your schemas? One-to-Many and Foreign Keys means place the pk of the one side as a foreign key in the many-side table, use not null if required, and declare referential constraints in ddl.. In practical terms, implement 1:n relationships with foreign key constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: 1:N → FK
keyIdea.text: Place the PK of the one side as a foreign key in the many-side table, use NOT NULL if required, and declare referential constraints in DDL.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › One-to-Many & Foreign Keys

Express one-to-many with foreign keys

Embed the parent's primary key on the child table and declare a FOREIGN KEY constraint to enforce integrity.

Pattern
  • Child table gets parent_id column.
  • Define NOT NULL if relation is mandatory.
  • Add FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES Parent(pk) to enforce integrity.
Example
CREATE TABLE Orders (
  order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  order_date DATE NOT NULL,
  total_amount DECIMAL(10,2),
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id)
);
Design Considerations
  • Decide cascade rules: ON DELETE CASCADE removes children when parent is deleted.
  • Use ON DELETE SET NULL if you need to retain child records but lose the parent link.
  • Index foreign keys if used in joins for performance.
Common Mistake
Not defining the FK constraint leaves referential integrity to application code, which is error-prone and can produce orphan rows.

screens.title: One-to-One Relationships
screens.narratorSegment: One-to-one relationships are less common but important when you split an entity into two tables for optional data or storage reasons. There are two common implementations: give one table a foreign key referencing the other with a UNIQUE constraint to ensure one-to-one cardinality, or share the primary key so the child table’s primary key is also a foreign key to the parent. For example, Employee and EmployeeDetails can be linked by making employee_id the primary key in both tables, where EmployeeDetails. employee_id is also a FOREIGN KEY referencing Employees(employee_id). This shared-key approach enforces that each details row maps to exactly one employee. A misconception is to rely on application logic to prevent multiple detail rows per employee; you need a UNIQUE constraint or a shared PK in DDL. Consider space and query patterns before splitting tables: sometimes separating rarely used columns into a details table improves performance, but it also complicates queries. Key takeaway: enforce 1:1 in DDL either with UNIQUE FK or by sharing PKs, and choose the pattern that best fits your access and storage needs. Which pattern will you choose for optional large attributes?

keyIdea.title: 1:1 Patterns
keyIdea.text: Use a UNIQUE foreign key or shared primary key to enforce one-to-one relationships and avoid relying on application checks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › One-to-One Relationships

Enforce 1:1 using UNIQUE FK or shared PK

Choose the implementation that fits your data access patterns and constraints.

Pattern A: UNIQUE FK
Add a foreign key column on the dependent table and make it UNIQUE to ensure a single partner per row.
Example
CREATE TABLE Employees (
  employee_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE EmployeeDetails (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  employee_id BIGINT UNIQUE,
  address VARCHAR(255),
  FOREIGN KEY (employee_id) REFERENCES Employees(employee_id)
);
Pattern B: Shared Primary Key
Use the parent primary key as the child's primary key so rows correspond one-to-one directly.
Example
CREATE TABLE EmployeeDetails (
  employee_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  address VARCHAR(255),
  phone_number VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE,
  FOREIGN KEY (employee_id) REFERENCES Employees(employee_id)
);

screens.title: Many-to-Many and Junction Tables
screens.narratorSegment: Many-to-many relationships cannot be expressed directly in a relational table; they require a junction table that stores associations between the two entities. The junction table includes foreign keys to both related entities and typically uses a composite primary key composed of those two foreign keys to prevent duplicate pairs. For example, Students and Courses are related through a StudentCourses table with student_id and course_id as foreign keys and a primary key (student_id, course_id). Additional attributes about the relationship, such as enrollment_date, belong in the junction table. A common misconception is trying to store arrays of foreign keys inside a single column; relational databases enforce relationships through joins and dedicated tables. Another pitfall is omitting a primary key on the junction table, which allows duplicate enrollments and undermines data integrity. Key takeaway: model many-to-many with a junction table, use composite primary keys for uniqueness, and include relationship attributes there. How will you model additional properties of relationships in your schemas? Many-to-Many and Junction Tables means represent many-to-many relationships as a junction table with fks to both entities and a composite primary key to enforce uniqueness.. In practical terms, resolve m:n relationships with a junction table and composite primary keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Junction Table
keyIdea.text: Represent many-to-many relationships as a junction table with FKs to both entities and a composite primary key to enforce uniqueness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Many-to-Many

Resolve M:N via junction tables

Create a distinct associative table with foreign keys to each side and a composite primary key to enforce unique pairings.

Pattern
  • Create a junction table with both foreign keys.
  • Use PRIMARY KEY (fk1, fk2) to prevent duplicate associations.
  • Place relationship attributes, such as enrollment_date, on the junction table.
Example DDL
CREATE TABLE Students (
  student_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  student_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE Courses (
  course_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  course_title VARCHAR(255)
);

CREATE TABLE StudentCourses (
  student_id BIGINT,
  course_id BIGINT,
  enrollment_date DATE NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES Students(student_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES Courses(course_id)
);
Design Notes
If you need surrogate keys for the junction table to support additional metadata or external referencing, add a separate id column while still enforcing uniqueness on the pair.
Common Mistake
Omitting the composite primary key allows duplicate relationships and leads to inconsistent reports.

screens.title: SQL Constraints for Data Integrity
screens.narratorSegment: S Q L constraints are the database’s way of enforcing rules so applications don’t have to catch every error. NOT NULL prevents missing values for critical fields such as names or borrowed dates. UNIQUE ensures no two rows share the same value, useful for emails or usernames. CHECK enforces a condition, for example CHECK (price >= 0) or CHECK (publication_year BETWEEN 1000 AND 2023) to validate ranges. DEFAULT provides a fallback value when none is supplied, for instance a borrowed_date defaulting to the current date. A concrete example: defining price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price > 0) and stock_quantity INT CHECK (stock_quantity >= 0) protects data from invalid inserts. A common misconception is that constraints slow down writes dramatically; reasonable constraints are a small cost compared to the cost of corrupted data and complex application-side checks. Another mistake is trying to validate complex business logic solely with CHECK; some rules belong in application logic or triggers. Key takeaway: use these constraints to make your schema self-validating and simpler to reason about. Which constraint will you add first to your next table?

keyIdea.title: Use Constraints
keyIdea.text: Apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT where appropriate to make the database enforce the rules of your domain.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › SQL Constraints

Enforce rules with DDL constraints

Apply the right constraints to keep data valid and predictable for applications and reports.

Constraint Quick Reference
  • NOT NULL: column must have a value.
  • UNIQUE: values must be distinct.
  • CHECK: expression must be true for each row.
  • DEFAULT: fallback value when omitted.
Example
CREATE TABLE Products (
  product_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  product_name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price > 0),
  stock_quantity INT DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock_quantity >= 0)
);
When to use each
NOT NULL: required fields the application relies on.
UNIQUE: alternate identifiers used for lookups.
CHECK: simple business rules enforceable in SQL.
DEFAULT: common values such as timestamps or counters.
Key Takeaway

Well-chosen constraints make your schema reliable and reduce application complexity.

screens.title: ALTER TABLE and Schema Evolution
screens.narratorSegment: ALTER TABLE is the DDL command you use to change table structures after creation. Common operations include adding or dropping columns, adding constraints, and creating or removing indexes. When altering large production tables, changes can be resource-intensive and may lock the table, so always test in a staging environment and plan maintenance windows. For example, adding a phone_number column is simple: ALTER TABLE Customers ADD COLUMN phone_number VARCHAR(20); but adding a CHECK constraint or a NOT NULL column with existing rows requires care — you may need to backfill values before enforcing NOT NULL. Another example: adding a format-checking constraint might use ALTER TABLE... ADD CONSTRAINT chk_phone_format CHECK (phone_number LIKE '[0-9]{10}'); but note that exact CHECK syntax can differ by DBMS. A common misconception is that ALTER TABLE is always cheap; it can be costly on large datasets. Key takeaway: use ALTER TABLE for schema evolution, but test and sequence changes safely: add nullable columns, backfill data, then add NOT NULL and CHECK constraints. How will you sequence your next schema change to avoid downtime? ALTER TABLE and Schema Evolution means use alter table to evolve schemas, but plan carefully: add nullable columns first, backfill, then enforce constraints to avoid locks and downtime.. In practical terms, safely add columns and constraints as requirements change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use ALTER TABLE to evolve schemas, but plan carefully: add nullable columns first, backfill, then enforce constraints to avoid locks and downtime.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › ALTER TABLE

Evolve table structures safely

Use ALTER TABLE to add columns and constraints, but sequence changes to avoid locking and data inconsistency.

Safe Sequence
  1. Add a nullable column.
  2. Backfill existing rows with appropriate values.
  3. Add NOT NULL or CHECK constraints once data complies.
  4. Index the column if it will be queried often.
Example
ALTER TABLE Customers
ADD COLUMN phone_number VARCHAR(20);
-- Backfill phone_number for existing rows
ALTER TABLE Customers
ALTER COLUMN phone_number SET NOT NULL;
Considerations
  • Test on copies of production data for performance impact.
  • Prefer online schema change tools for large tables when available.
  • Document schema migrations and maintain rollback plans.
Common Mistake
Adding a NOT NULL constraint without backfilling causes the ALTER to fail or produce inconsistent data if the DB disallows it.

screens.title: Library Schema DDL — Full CREATE TABLE Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the library schema hands-on. The Book table uses ISBN as a natural primary key; choose VARCHAR(13) to store ISBN values and enforce title and author as NOT NULL. Add a CHECK on publication_year to keep values sensible. The Member table needs a surrogate member_id with AUTO_INCREMENT for internal joins and name as NOT NULL. The Loan table is the junction/associative entity that links Book and Member: it has a loan_id surrogate primary key, ISBN as a foreign key, member_id as a foreign key, borrowed_date required, returned_date optional, and a default for borrowed_date set to the current date. When you write CREATE TABLE statements, include FOREIGN KEY clauses so the database rejects orphan loan records. A common mistake is omitting the CHECK on publication_year or forgetting NOT NULL on borrowed_date. After creating these tables, test with sample INSERTs and use DESCRIBE or show create table to validate columns and constraints. Key takeaway: implement entity tables, then create the associative table with proper FK constraints and defaults. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Library DDL Walkthrough

CREATE TABLE for Book, Member, and Loan

Use the starter template and complete it with types, PKs, FKs, NOT NULL, CHECK, and DEFAULT clauses.

Starter DDL (complete)
CREATE TABLE Book (
  ISBN VARCHAR(13) PRIMARY KEY,
  title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  author VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  publication_year INT,
  CHECK (publication_year BETWEEN 1000 AND 2023)
);

CREATE TABLE Member (
  member_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  address VARCHAR(500)
);

CREATE TABLE Loan (
  loan_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  ISBN VARCHAR(13) NOT NULL,
  member_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  borrowed_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE NOT NULL,
  returned_date DATE,
  FOREIGN KEY (ISBN) REFERENCES Book(ISBN),
  FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES Member(member_id)
);
Checks & Tests
After creating tables, insert representative rows and verify the DB rejects invalid data, such as a Loan referencing a non-existent ISBN or a Book with a publication year outside the allowed range.
Key Takeaway

Translate ERD entities into tables, enforce relationships with FKs, and protect domain rules with NOT NULL, CHECK, and DEFAULT constraints.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: When translating ER models to DDL, several common mistakes recur. Forgetting NOT NULL on essential fields allows incomplete records and forces application-side checks. Choosing incorrect data types can lead to truncation or wasted space; for example, using VARCHAR(1000) for short identifiers is inefficient. Missing foreign key constraints results in orphaned child rows and inconsistent reports. Improperly resolving many-to-many relationships without a junction table will break normalization. Beyond correctness, consider performance: primary keys create indexes, but additional frequently queried columns may need indexes too. Over-indexing can slow writes, so balance read needs against write cost. A practical approach is to create keys and FKs first, run representative queries, then add indexes for slow patterns. Also, be mindful of ALTER TABLE costs when planning migrations for large tables. A useful misconception check: assume indexes fix slow queries — they help read performance but add write overhead and must be chosen strategically. Key takeaway: enforce integrity in DDL, choose types carefully, and plan an indexing strategy informed by query patterns. What’s the first performance metric you would check after creating a schema? In practical terms, avoid integrity gaps and plan indexing as part of schema design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Common Mistakes & Performance

Avoid integrity gaps; plan indexes thoughtfully

Correctness and performance go hand-in-hand — enforce integrity first, then profile and add indexes as needed.

Top Mistakes
  • Missing NOT NULL on required attributes.
  • Incorrect data types causing truncation or overflow.
  • Missing FK constraints leading to orphaned records.
  • Not using a junction table for many-to-many relationships.
Performance Tips
  • Primary keys are indexed automatically; add indexes for frequent lookups.
  • Avoid over-indexing to keep write performance acceptable.
  • Profile queries on representative data before adding indexes.
Practical Check

After creation, run sample queries and check execution plans to guide index decisions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These core concepts are the practical rules you should carry forward. First, S Q L DDL is how your ER model becomes a physical schema: CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE express structure and changes. Second, primary keys and foreign keys enforce identity and referential integrity across tables; use surrogate keys when you need stable numeric identifiers and enforce business uniqueness separately. Third, choose S Q L data types that match the nature and range of values — DECIMAL for money, TIMESTAMP for events, VARCHAR for bounded text. Fourth, constraints like NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT make the database self-validating, reducing application complexity. Fifth, many-to-many relationships require junction tables with composite keys or surrogate IDs plus uniqueness. Finally, schema evolution via ALTER TABLE must be planned and tested. Keep these concepts in mind as you write DDL and validate with sample INSERTs and schema inspections. Which concept will you apply first when creating a new schema?

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we move from abstract modeling to a working database schema. You'll learn how each entity and attribute in your ER diagram becomes a table and column, and how relationships turn into primary and foreign key constraints. Choosing the right S Q L data types is essential: they affect storage, precision, and query performance. We'll also cover constraints — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT — so the database enforces the rules you designed in the ERD. Concrete examples from customer-orders, employees, students-courses, and a library loan scenario show how to express one-to-many, one-to-one, and many-to-many relationships in DDL. Finally, you'll see how ALTER TABLE supports safe schema evolution and common pitfalls to avoid, such as missing foreign keys or incorrect data types. By the end of this lesson you will be able to write clear CREATE TABLE statements, pick suitable types, and implement keys and constraints so your schema is both correct and performant. Consider how the rules you add now will prevent application bugs later. Which integrity rule do you expect to be most important for your next schema?

These objectives map directly to the practical steps you will take converting ER models into real tables. First, you will translate entities into tables and attributes into columns, choosing types that match expected values and scale. Second, you will convert ERD relationships into primary and foreign key constraints so referential integrity is enforced by the DBMS, handling common patterns like one-to-many, one-to-one, and many-to-many with junction tables. Third, you'll select S Q L data types appropriately — integers of the right size, precise decimals for money, and timestamp types for temporal data — to balance space and correctness. Fourth, you'll write CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE statements and apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT constraints to ensure the data meets business rules. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help remember when to use the pattern, and the verified competency milestone points to writing correct DDL for a simple library schema. Practicing these skills reduces runtime errors and prevents inconsistent data in applications. Which objective will you practice first?

These applied objectives show how you will use DDL in real scenarios. You will write CREATE TABLE statements for entities and specify NOT NULL for required fields like names or dates so applications can rely on consistent records. You will convert ERD relationships: place a foreign key on the many side for one-to-many patterns, use a unique foreign key for one-to-one, and create junction tables with composite primary keys for many-to-many. You will choose data types like BIGINT for global identifiers or DECIMAL for exact monetary values and apply CHECK constraints to guard against invalid values such as negative prices or out-of-range years. Finally, you will evolve schemas safely with ALTER TABLE, adding columns or constraints after testing in development. Each skill ties directly to the hands-on activity for a library system, where you'll write full CREATE TABLE statements and add checks and defaults. Practicing these tasks helps you catch integration bugs earlier and makes your schema self-documenting. Which applied objective will you try in the lab?

Mapping entities to tables is the first concrete step when implementing an ER model. An entity becomes a table and each attribute becomes a column. Begin by choosing clear table names that reflect the modeled concept — for example Customers or Book — and use consistent column naming for keys like customer_id or ISBN. Decide which attributes are mandatory and add NOT NULL to those columns; fields such as title or borrowed_date are often required. Choose a primary key for each table: this can be a natural key like ISBN or a surrogate key like an auto-incrementing identifier. A practical example is the Book entity: map ISBN to a VARCHAR primary key of length 13, set title and author to VARCHAR with NOT NULL, and add a CHECK to ensure the publication year is valid. A common misconception is treating every attribute as nullable by default; required business fields should be NOT NULL to prevent incomplete records. Another pitfall is overusing TEXT or very large types where a bounded VARCHAR would be more efficient. Key takeaway: map entities systematically, apply NOT NULL for required attributes, and choose keys early so relationships can reference them. How will you name keys in your next schema?

Selecting data types is a balance between storage efficiency, precision, and correctness. Use integer types like INT or BIGINT for whole numbers; choose based on expected range — INT is fine for moderate ranges, BIGINT for very large global identifiers. For exact numeric values such as money, use DECIMAL or NUMERIC with a fixed precision and scale; floating-point types like FLOAT or REAL introduce rounding and are not recommended for financial data. Text attributes use VARCHAR with a reasonable upper bound, or TEXT where length is unpredictable. For temporal data pick DATE for dates only, TIME for time-only values, and TIMESTAMP or DATETIME for combined date-time; prefer timestamp types that include timezone when tracking global events. A concrete example: product price should be DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL; a username can be VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL. A common misconception is overusing the largest types by default; this wastes storage and can hide range problems until runtime. Another trap is using FLOAT for money, causing subtle calculation errors. Key takeaway: choose the smallest type that safely fits expected values and enforces necessary precision. What attributes in your schema need stricter precision controls?

Primary keys uniquely identify rows and are central to relational integrity. A natural key is derived from domain data — for example ISBN uniquely identifies a book. A surrogate key is an artificial identifier, typically an auto-incrementing integer or serial. Surrogate keys simplify joins and can improve index performance, but they add an extra column and require a UNIQUE constraint on any natural identifier you still want to enforce. In many large systems, a BIGINT surrogate key is common because it avoids future overflow. Implementing auto-increment uses DBMS-specific features such as AUTO_INCREMENT, SERIAL, or IDENTITY. A concrete example: a Customers table might include customer_id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY while still marking email as UNIQUE NOT NULL. Misconceptions include thinking surrogate keys hide bad natural keys — surrogate keys are for identity, not for replacing unique business constraints. Another pitfall is using small integer types for IDs that will grow beyond their range. Key takeaway: choose a stable primary key strategy and enforce uniqueness on any business identifiers separately. How will you balance natural readability and long-term scalability in your keys?

One-to-many relationships are common: a single customer places many orders. To implement this, put the primary key of the one side into the many side as a foreign key. The foreign key column should be NOT NULL if every child row must relate to a parent, and you should add an explicit FOREIGN KEY constraint referencing the parent's primary key. This allows the DBMS to enforce referential integrity and prevents orphaned child rows. An example from the chapter: Orders includes customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL and a FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id). A practical misconception is assuming client code will prevent orphaned rows; without the FK, application bugs can create inconsistent data. Also consider cascade behaviors: ON DELETE CASCADE or ON DELETE SET NULL are decisions that affect data retention and must be chosen to match business rules. Key takeaway: model referential integrity in DDL using foreign keys, and explicitly decide cascading rules rather than relying on application logic. How will you handle deletions in your schemas? One-to-Many and Foreign Keys means place the pk of the one side as a foreign key in the many-side table, use not null if required, and declare referential constraints in ddl.. In practical terms, implement 1:n relationships with foreign key constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One-to-one relationships are less common but important when you split an entity into two tables for optional data or storage reasons. There are two common implementations: give one table a foreign key referencing the other with a UNIQUE constraint to ensure one-to-one cardinality, or share the primary key so the child table’s primary key is also a foreign key to the parent. For example, Employee and EmployeeDetails can be linked by making employee_id the primary key in both tables, where EmployeeDetails. employee_id is also a FOREIGN KEY referencing Employees(employee_id). This shared-key approach enforces that each details row maps to exactly one employee. A misconception is to rely on application logic to prevent multiple detail rows per employee; you need a UNIQUE constraint or a shared PK in DDL. Consider space and query patterns before splitting tables: sometimes separating rarely used columns into a details table improves performance, but it also complicates queries. Key takeaway: enforce 1:1 in DDL either with UNIQUE FK or by sharing PKs, and choose the pattern that best fits your access and storage needs. Which pattern will you choose for optional large attributes?

Many-to-many relationships cannot be expressed directly in a relational table; they require a junction table that stores associations between the two entities. The junction table includes foreign keys to both related entities and typically uses a composite primary key composed of those two foreign keys to prevent duplicate pairs. For example, Students and Courses are related through a StudentCourses table with student_id and course_id as foreign keys and a primary key (student_id, course_id). Additional attributes about the relationship, such as enrollment_date, belong in the junction table. A common misconception is trying to store arrays of foreign keys inside a single column; relational databases enforce relationships through joins and dedicated tables. Another pitfall is omitting a primary key on the junction table, which allows duplicate enrollments and undermines data integrity. Key takeaway: model many-to-many with a junction table, use composite primary keys for uniqueness, and include relationship attributes there. How will you model additional properties of relationships in your schemas? Many-to-Many and Junction Tables means represent many-to-many relationships as a junction table with fks to both entities and a composite primary key to enforce uniqueness.. In practical terms, resolve m:n relationships with a junction table and composite primary keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

S Q L constraints are the database’s way of enforcing rules so applications don’t have to catch every error. NOT NULL prevents missing values for critical fields such as names or borrowed dates. UNIQUE ensures no two rows share the same value, useful for emails or usernames. CHECK enforces a condition, for example CHECK (price >= 0) or CHECK (publication_year BETWEEN 1000 AND 2023) to validate ranges. DEFAULT provides a fallback value when none is supplied, for instance a borrowed_date defaulting to the current date. A concrete example: defining price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price > 0) and stock_quantity INT CHECK (stock_quantity >= 0) protects data from invalid inserts. A common misconception is that constraints slow down writes dramatically; reasonable constraints are a small cost compared to the cost of corrupted data and complex application-side checks. Another mistake is trying to validate complex business logic solely with CHECK; some rules belong in application logic or triggers. Key takeaway: use these constraints to make your schema self-validating and simpler to reason about. Which constraint will you add first to your next table?

ALTER TABLE is the DDL command you use to change table structures after creation. Common operations include adding or dropping columns, adding constraints, and creating or removing indexes. When altering large production tables, changes can be resource-intensive and may lock the table, so always test in a staging environment and plan maintenance windows. For example, adding a phone_number column is simple: ALTER TABLE Customers ADD COLUMN phone_number VARCHAR(20); but adding a CHECK constraint or a NOT NULL column with existing rows requires care — you may need to backfill values before enforcing NOT NULL. Another example: adding a format-checking constraint might use ALTER TABLE... ADD CONSTRAINT chk_phone_format CHECK (phone_number LIKE '[0-9]{10}'); but note that exact CHECK syntax can differ by DBMS. A common misconception is that ALTER TABLE is always cheap; it can be costly on large datasets. Key takeaway: use ALTER TABLE for schema evolution, but test and sequence changes safely: add nullable columns, backfill data, then add NOT NULL and CHECK constraints. How will you sequence your next schema change to avoid downtime? ALTER TABLE and Schema Evolution means use alter table to evolve schemas, but plan carefully: add nullable columns first, backfill, then enforce constraints to avoid locks and downtime.. In practical terms, safely add columns and constraints as requirements change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Let's walk through the library schema hands-on. The Book table uses ISBN as a natural primary key; choose VARCHAR(13) to store ISBN values and enforce title and author as NOT NULL. Add a CHECK on publication_year to keep values sensible. The Member table needs a surrogate member_id with AUTO_INCREMENT for internal joins and name as NOT NULL. The Loan table is the junction/associative entity that links Book and Member: it has a loan_id surrogate primary key, ISBN as a foreign key, member_id as a foreign key, borrowed_date required, returned_date optional, and a default for borrowed_date set to the current date. When you write CREATE TABLE statements, include FOREIGN KEY clauses so the database rejects orphan loan records. A common mistake is omitting the CHECK on publication_year or forgetting NOT NULL on borrowed_date. After creating these tables, test with sample INSERTs and use DESCRIBE or show create table to validate columns and constraints. Key takeaway: implement entity tables, then create the associative table with proper FK constraints and defaults. When translating ER models to DDL, several common mistakes recur. Forgetting NOT NULL on essential fields allows incomplete records and forces application-side checks. Choosing incorrect data types can lead to truncation or wasted space; for example, using VARCHAR(1000) for short identifiers is inefficient. Missing foreign key constraints results in orphaned child rows and inconsistent reports. Improperly resolving many-to-many relationships without a junction table will break normalization. Beyond correctness, consider performance: primary keys create indexes, but additional frequently queried columns may need indexes too. Over-indexing can slow writes, so balance read needs against write cost. A practical approach is to create keys and FKs first, run representative queries, then add indexes for slow patterns. Also, be mindful of ALTER TABLE costs when planning migrations for large tables. A useful misconception check: assume indexes fix slow queries — they help read performance but add write overhead and must be chosen strategically. Key takeaway: enforce integrity in DDL, choose types carefully, and plan an indexing strategy informed by query patterns. What’s the first performance metric you would check after creating a schema? Common Mistakes and Performance Considerations means don't skip not null or foreign keys, choose appropriate types, and plan indexes after observing real query patterns to balance read/write performance.. These core concepts are the practical rules you should carry forward. First, S Q L DDL is how your ER model becomes a physical schema: CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE express structure and changes. Second, primary keys and foreign keys enforce identity and referential integrity across tables; use surrogate keys when you need stable numeric identifiers and enforce business uniqueness separately. Third, choose S Q L data types that match the nature and range of values — DECIMAL for money, TIMESTAMP for events, VARCHAR for bounded text. Fourth, constraints like NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT make the database self-validating, reducing application complexity. Fifth, many-to-many relationships require junction tables with composite keys or surrogate IDs plus uniqueness. Finally, schema evolution via ALTER TABLE must be planned and tested. Keep these concepts in mind as you write DDL and validate with sample INSERTs and schema inspections. Which concept will you apply first when creating a new schema?

Keep these three concise reminders when implementing DDL. First, always make the database enforce integrity: primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints reduce application bugs. Second, choose types deliberately: size, precision, and semantics matter for correctness and performance. Third, plan schema changes: use ALTER TABLE carefully, backfill data before enforcing NOT NULL, and test changes on representative data. These practices produce schemas that are maintainable, performant, and aligned with your ER model.
